CHAPTER 3 
STATUTES OF FRAUDS 
I. BACKGROUND 
Plaintiffs obtained a $276,000.00 loan ("Loan") that they used to 
urchase real property in Sugar Land, Texas. The Loan was evidenced 
hy a Promissory Note and was secured by a Deed of Trust. Plaintiffs 
defaulted on their payment obligations under the Promissory Note, and 
the property was sold in a foreclosure sale in April 2011. 
Plaintiffs filed this lawsuit in Texas state court in September 2011, 
seeking to delay post foreclosure eviction proceedings. ln addition to 
seeking injunctive relief, Plaintiffs asserted claims for fraud, wrongful 
foreclosure due to fraud,

promissory estop el claim based on Defendant's alleged promise not to 
foreclose during a loan modification process. 
III. ANALYSIS 
B. Statute of Frauds and Promissory Estoppel 
Plaintiffs allege that Defendant 
promised not to foreclose on the 
property during a loan modification review proces . Under Texas law, th 
statute of frauds requires all loan agreements involving more than 
$50,000.00 to bl' in writing and signed by the party to be bound in order 
to be enforceable. See TEX. BUS. & COM. CODE § 26.02(b).b A "loan 
agreement" for purposes of the statute of frauds is defined to include 
promises by a financial institution to "delay repayment of money ... or 
make a financial accommodation." See TEX. BUS. & COM. CODE 
§ 26.02(a)(2).c Plaintiffs' claim that Defendant promised 
to make a 
financial accommodation by delaying foreclosure is barred by the Texas 
statute of frauds. See Burnette v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 2010 WL 
1026968, *5 (E.D. Tex. Feb. 16, 2010) (quoting Krudop v. Bridge City 
State Bank, 2006 WL 3627078, *4 (Tex. App.-Beaumont Dec. 14, 2006, 
pet. denied)). 
Promissory estoppel, whether asserted as an affirmative claim or as 
a de_fense to the i:;tatute of frauds, requires that the "promisor promised 
to sign a written document that would satisfy the statute of frauds."
